The space station, known as the Aethelgard Outpost, hung in the silent void like a forgotten tooth in the jaw of the cosmos. It orbited the planet designated as Xylos-9, a world stripped of atmosphere and life by the Great Silencing three centuries prior. The planet’s surface was a monochrome expanse of gray dust and jagged obsidian shards, reflecting the cold, distant light of a dying red dwarf star. There was no wind, no sound, no movement—only the eternal, crushing stillness of a dead world.

The station itself was a relic of the Pre-Collapse Era, a time when humanity had reached for the stars with both hands open. Built during the height of the Interstellar Expansion, the Aethelgard was originally a mining hub, designed to extract rare isotopes from the asteroid belt that now performed its eerie ballet outside the viewing ports. Those asteroids were not merely rocks; they were the shattered remnants of a moon that had been torn apart by gravitational anomalies during the Collapse. Their dance was a slow, gravitational waltz, each fragment tracing an elliptical path that had been unbroken for generations.

Inside, the metallic corridors of the station were a labyrinth of rusted bulkheads and flickering luminescent strips. The hum of machinery was not just sound; it was the heartbeat of a dying beast. The life support systems, ancient and overworked, groaned under the strain of maintaining breathable air for the handful of survivors who called this place home. These survivors were the descendants of the original crew, their lineage diluted by time and isolation. They spoke in hushed tones, their voices echoing off the cold metal walls, carrying the weight of a history that had been erased from the rest of the galaxy.

The historical context of the Aethelgard is one of abandonment and resilience. When the Collapse occurred, the central government of the human colonies fell into chaos, communication lines severed, and supply routes cut off. The Aethelgard, located on the fringe of known space, was left to fend for itself. Over the centuries, the station became a microcosm of human society, with its own rules, its own culture, and its own myths. The asteroids outside were not just celestial bodies; they were symbols of the fragility of existence, a constant reminder that even the most solid things could be shattered by forces beyond control.
